title: Like a dream and a show
hookLine: know this world like a dream and a show; none of it is true without the Lord (Salok M9, ang 1427)
last: FEAR NONE — FRIGHTEN NONE, FEAR NONE.

cards: You're in a dream, and it's urgent. You've missed the exam, or the train is leaving, or you're back at an old school and can't find the classroom. Your heart is pounding.
It's completely real. Then your eyes open. The ceiling.
The alarm clock. Your own bed. In about three seconds the whole drama drains away, and you almost laugh.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok asks what it would be like to see the whole world with those first waking eyes.

teach.b: The salok says jio supnaa ar pekhnaa, aise jag kau jaan. In paraphrase: like a dream and a show, know the world to be so. In all of it, nothing is saacho, true, says Nanak, except the Lord.

teach.h: PEKHNAA: A SHOW ON A STREET.
teach.b: Pekhnaa is a show, a spectacle, the kind of street play or puppet performance a crowd gathers to watch. It's vivid, it pulls you in, you might even cry. Then the curtain drops and everyone goes home.

This salok needs to be heard alongside the rest of the Granth. In Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says the Lord is true, and everything He has made is true. So Sikh teaching doesn't call the world a lie in the sense of fake.

teach.h: TRUE AS HIS, PASSING AS A DREAM.
teach.b: Both lines are in the same scripture, and Sikh teachers hold them together: the world is real as the Lord's creation, and passing as a dream is passing. Read beside Sukhmani, saacho here points to what lasts.
What isn't true is our grip on the world, taking the show for the whole of reality. Now go back to yesterday's courage.
Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur facing the empire's threats in Delhi without fear, and some readers hear this salok as part of the reason: he saw those threats with waking eyes.
Real, and terrible, but not the thing that lasts.
The dream isn't worthless. It just isn't the place to build your whole life. Wake up inside it, and you can play your part in the show without forgetting it's a show.

how: Sikhs hear this salok at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; teachers often read it beside Guru Arjan's line that the Lord is true and all He made is true, so that the world is honored and held lightly at once.

o: a street show a crowd gathers for
a dream, vivid while it lasts

games.q: like a dream and a show — tap the pairs.

s: in Sikh teaching, the world is simply fake
the Granth calls the Lord's creation true and also passing like a dream; teachers hold both.
the salok compares the world to a show that ends
pekhnaa: vivid while it lasts, then the curtain drops.
the salok says nothing in the world is true except the Lord
in mai kachh saacho nahee: nothing in it is true, says Nanak, except the Lord; teachers hear 'true' here as 'lasting'.

games.q: you wake from a vivid dream, heart still pounding. how does the salok want you to see the world?
o: as a lie, so nothing matters.
like a dream and a show: real while it lasts, and passing.
as the only thing that's real.
games.why: jio supnaa ar pekhnaa, aise jag kau jaan: know the world like a dream and a show. nothing in it is true, says Nanak, except the Lord.

practice: Close your eyes and recall any dream, last night's or any vivid one, even a fragment, and notice how real it felt and how quickly it faded on waking.

Then open your eyes and look around the room with the same fresh, waking eyes: the chair, the light, your hands, real and passing. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, the One the salok says remains.

wordCard.voice: Supnaa, a dream. The salok asks us to know the world like supnaa, and pekhnaa, a show: vivid, real while it lasts, and passing, while the Lord remains.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: supnaa, a dream. The salok pairs it with pekhnaa, a show.

carryVoice: Your line: like a dream. Waking eyes can still love the show. That's day five hundred ninety-six.
